sections.section_title: Pointwise Multiplication of X(j\omega) and H(j\omega)

example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the magnitudes multiply to $6$ and the phase terms combine to give $Y(j\omega)=6e^{j(\omega/2-\pi/6)}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete product after the rule, so the only new work is carrying out the multiplication and combining the exponential factors correctly.

sections.section_title: Choosing Time-Domain Convolution for Overlap and Support Questions
sections.learning_goal: Use time-domain convolution to reason about support and overlap directly when the signals have finite duration.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step uses finite-support symbolic signals only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five labeled choices A-E; one choice names the clearer domain for support and overlap reasoning.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which domain gives the quickest route to the support of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ when $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ are finite-duration pulses?
distractor_plan: Include frequency domain as the tempting but less direct choice.
Include a 'both domains' option as a hedge.
Include a choice that confuses support with amplitude or height.
Include a choice that claims the answer is only obvious after transforming first.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For finite-duration signals such as $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$, decide whether the time domain is the clearest route and determine the support of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that overlap and support are easiest to read by sliding one pulse across the other in time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same convolution output but adds a task whose key feature is finite support and overlap rather than symbol matching.
solution_step_plan: Identify the support of $x(t)$ and $h(t)$.
Reason about when the shifted pulses overlap.
Combine the supports to determine the nonzero interval for $y(t)$.
State why the time domain is the clearest tool for this question.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pulse widths while keeping finite support.
Shift one pulse in time and ask for the new overlap interval.
Ask for the domain choice before asking for the support interval.
Replace rectangles with another compactly supported waveform.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the support argument concrete and geometric in time; do not drift into spectral algebra.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Domain Multiplication for Algebraic Computation
sections.learning_goal: Use frequency-domain multiplication to simplify computation when $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ are algebraic expressions.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step is an algebraic frequency-domain comparison.

question_policy.answer_format: Five labeled choices A-E; one choice names the clearer domain or the correct product form for $Y(j\omega)$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which domain gives the quickest route to $Y(j\omega)$ when $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ are simple algebraic expressions?
distractor_plan: Include time-domain convolution as the most plausible but slower alternative.
Include a choice that mistakes the task for support reasoning.
Include a choice that describes interpretation instead of computation.
Include a choice that treats the product as a sum or ratio.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For spectra such as $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{2}{1-j\omega}$, decide whether the frequency domain is the clearer route and compute $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that multiplying the spectra is easier than forming the time-domain convolution and that the output spectrum follows immediately from the product.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same output comparison but shifts from support reasoning to algebraic simplification in the frequency domain.
solution_step_plan: Identify the spectra as the direct inputs to the product rule.
Multiply $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ symbolically.
Simplify the resulting rational expression.
Note that the time-domain convolution would be more cumbersome.
practice_variation_axes: Change the algebraic form of one spectrum while preserving a simple product.
Use a low-pass or band-pass transfer function as one factor.
Ask which domain is easier before asking for the product.
Add a scalar gain or a simple conjugate-style factor to the product.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example algebraic; the value of the frequency domain should be obvious from the arithmetic.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Clearer Domain for Interpreting an LTI Output
sections.learning_goal: Choose the clearer domain for interpreting what an LTI output means, not just for computing it.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the step interprets spectral filtering symbolically.

question_policy.answer_format: Five labeled choices A-E; one choice names the clearer domain and the main interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which domain gives the clearest interpretation of an LTI output when $H(j\omega)$ acts as a low-pass filter on $X(j\omega)$?
distractor_plan: Include time domain as the tempting choice because the final output is still a waveform.
Include a 'both domains' option that avoids committing to the clearer interpretation.
Include a choice that focuses on support or overlap instead of spectral filtering.
Include a choice that says the frequency domain is useful but does not connect it to interpretation.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An input $x(t)$ has several frequency components and $H(j\omega)$ strongly attenuates the high-frequency components. Decide which domain is clearer for interpreting the output and explain what the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ says about $y(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the frequency domain is the clearest interpretation tool when the question is about filtering, attenuation, or spectral shaping.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from computation to interpretation while keeping the same time-versus-frequency choice.
solution_step_plan: Identify what feature of the output the question is really asking about.
Read the effect of $H(j\omega)$ on the spectrum $X(j\omega)$.
Infer the impact on the output waveform from the spectral change.
State why the frequency domain gives the clearest explanation here.
practice_variation_axes: Change the system to a notch, band-pass, or low-pass response.
Change the input so one spectral region dominates.
Ask for the clearer domain before asking for the interpretation.
Ask for the qualitative output effect rather than a numeric computation.

sections.handoff_notes: End with the domain-choice rule applied to interpretation, not just arithmetic.

entries.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
entries.lesson_core_move: Trace the proof idea of the convolution theorem by substituting the convolution integral into the Fourier transform definition, interchanging integration order, and recognizing the two individual spectra.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.learning_goal: Set up the theorem proof as a symbolic rewrite from the convolution integral to the product of spectra.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State the theorem target: rewrite the Fourier transform of $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$ until it becomes $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from one continuous-time LTI output $y(t)$ and the Fourier transform definition.
paragraph_plan: State the target identity in notation the learner already knows.
Recall the convolution integral and the Fourier transform definition as the two ingredients that will be combined.
Preview the algebraic path: substitute, rewrite as a double integral, swap integration order, and recognize the factors.
Keep the focus on the proof idea rather than on formal convergence details.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable; this opening section only sets up the proof idea before the first substitution example.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Set up the theorem target before the worked algebra begins.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This opening section does not solve a worked example; it simply orients the learner to the proof path.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opener lean. The next section should move immediately into substitution.

sections.section_title: Substituting the Convolution Integral into the Fourier Transform
sections.learning_goal: Substitute the convolution integral into the Fourier transform of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ without changing variables yet.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct substitution.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which expression correctly rewrites $Y(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(x*h)(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ after substituting the convolution definition?
distractor_plan: Omit the inner convolution integral and leave $(x*h)(t)$ unchanged.
Move $e^{-j\omega t}$ inside the convolution integral before the substitution is made.
Replace the convolution with pointwise multiplication too early.
Swap $t$ and $\tau$ or change the sign in $h(t-\tau)$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the first algebraic move is to replace $(x*h)(t)$ with its integral definition inside $Y(j\omega)$.
paragraph_plan: Restate the output transform with $y(t)$ written as $(x*h)(t)$.
Substitute $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ for the convolution term.
Keep the two nested integrals visible and do not simplify yet.
Prepare the learner for the next step, where the nested structure is made explicit.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Start from $Y(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(x*h)(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ and substitute the convolution integral for $(x*h)(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Obtain the nested-integration form without changing variables or swapping the order yet.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first algebraic step after the theorem statement, so the only new move is inserting the convolution definition into the transform definition.
solution_step_plan: Write $(x*h)(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.
Replace $(x*h)(t)$ inside the Fourier transform integral.
Leave the result as a double integral to set up the next rewrite.
practice_variation_axes: Change the input/output notation but keep the same convolution substitution.
Vary the symbol used for the dummy variable while keeping the structure intact.
Keep the transform definition fixed and ask the learner to identify the correct substitution.

sections.handoff_notes: No order swap yet. The worked example should stop after the substitution is visible as a double integral.

sections.section_title: Rewriting the Transform as an Iterated Integral
sections.learning_goal: Rewrite the substituted transform as a double integral with clearly separated $t$ and $\tau$ roles.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct iterated-integral rewrite.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which expression is the correct iterated-integral rewrite of the substituted Fourier transform?
distractor_plan: Collapse the two integrals into one and lose the nested structure.
Pull the exponential into the wrong integral or attach it to the wrong variable.
Rename the dummy variables but break the meaning of the inner vs. outer integral.
Rewrite the expression as a product before integration order is changed.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Make the iterated-integral structure explicit so the learner can see which variable belongs to the outer transform and which belongs to the convolution.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from the already-substituted expression in section 2.
paragraph_plan: Rewrite the nested integral with both integration variables visible.
Keep the exponential factor attached to the outer transform variable.
Name the dummy variables carefully so the learner can track the roles of $t$ and $\tau$.
Point out that no algebra has been completed yet; this is only a structural rewrite.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite the substituted Fourier transform as an iterated integral with respect to $\tau$ and $t$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Make the double-integral structure explicit so the next step can justify exchanging the order of integration.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The only new wrinkle is reorganizing the same integrand into a clear iterated-integral format.
solution_step_plan: Carry the exponential factor $e^{-j\omega t}$ through the outer integral.
Write the convolution integral inside the transform integral.
Display the result as a double integral with clear bounds and dummy variables.
practice_variation_axes: Present the same double integral with renamed dummy variables.
Vary the order in which the factors are written inside the integrand.
Ask the learner to identify the expression that is actually an iterated integral rather than a single integral.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the algebra structural; the point is to see the iterated integral before any factorization.

sections.section_title: Interchanging the Order of Integration
sections.learning_goal: Swap the order of integration to isolate the factor that depends only on $\tau$ outside the inner $t$-integral.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct order-swap rewrite.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which rewritten form correctly interchanges the order of integration in the substituted transform expression?
distractor_plan: Swap the order but leave one factor inside the wrong integral.
Change the integration limits incorrectly when moving from one order to the other.
Skip the structural rewrite and jump directly to the final product $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
Treat the integrand as if it were separable before the shift factor is exposed.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Explain that the double integral can be read in the opposite order, and that doing so positions the shifted impulse response for recognition.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the iterated integral from section 3.
paragraph_plan: State the integrand in a form where the $t$- and $\tau$-dependence are visible.
Swap the order of integration while keeping the same integrand and bounds.
Explain why this step matters: it positions the shift-dependent term so the inner integral becomes recognizable.
Keep the justification conceptual and avoid formal convergence arguments.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Take the iterated integral for $Y(j\omega)$ and interchange the order of integration so the $t$-integral sits inside.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Rewrite the expression so one factor depends only on $\tau$ outside the inner integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The new wrinkle is the change in integration order; no new transform pair is introduced yet.
solution_step_plan: Move $x(\tau)$ outside the inner $t$-integral.
Keep $h(t-\tau)e^{-j\omega t}$ inside the $t$-integral.
Rewrite the expression with the $\tau$-integral outside and the $t$-integral inside.
practice_variation_axes: Ask the learner to swap the order on a slightly differently written double integral.
Vary the placement of the constant factor outside the inner integral.
Use a different dummy-variable name for the outer variable while keeping the same structure.

sections.handoff_notes: The point of this step is structural, not evaluative: the learner should see the inner transform-like expression emerge.

sections.section_title: Exposing the Shifted Transform Factor
sections.learning_goal: Use a change of variables in the inner integral to expose the shifted Fourier transform factor.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct change-of-variables rewrite.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which change-of-variables rewrite correctly exposes the shifted transform factor inside the inner integral?
distractor_plan: Use the wrong sign in the substitution $u=t\pm\tau$.
Drop the shift-dependent exponential factor after the change of variables.
Mistake the inner integral for the wrong transform factor.
Stop before isolating the remaining Fourier transform term.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show the substitution that turns $h(t-\tau)e^{-j\omega t}$ into a transform-like factor with a shift exponential.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from the swapped-order expression with $x(\tau)$ outside the inner $t$-integral.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the change of variables that removes the shift from $h(t-\tau)$.
Factor out the exponential term that depends only on the shift variable.
Identify the remaining inner integral as the transform of $h(t)$ or an equivalent shifted version.
Keep the notation consistent so the final product recognition in the next step is easy.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: In the inner integral, make the substitution $u=t-\tau$ and expose the factor that carries the shift dependence.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Rewrite the inner integral as $e^{-j\omega \tau}H(j\omega)$, or an equivalent shifted-transform factor, before combining it with the outer integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This step adds a genuine new algebraic wrinkle: a change of variables inside the nested integral.
solution_step_plan: Let $u=t-\tau$ so $t=u+\tau$ and $dt=du$.
Pull out the factor that depends only on $\tau$.
Recognize the remaining integral as $H(j\omega)$ or the matching spectrum factor.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the shift variable while keeping the same substitution structure.
Use a different impulse-response symbol but the same change of variables.
Ask the learner to identify the expression after substitution rather than to carry out every algebraic line.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the variable substitution explicit and keep the factorization readable.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Product of the Two Individual Spectra
sections.learning_goal: Recognize the outer integral and exposed factor as $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, then state the convolution theorem.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct factorization and theorem statement.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which final identification correctly turns the factorized expression into the convolution theorem statement?
distractor_plan: Name only one factor and leave the other unidentified.
Multiply the spectra in the wrong domain or in the wrong order.
State addition instead of multiplication.
Treat the final expression as if it were still a single integral.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that after the shift factor is exposed, the remaining outer integral is exactly the Fourier transform of $x(t)$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the expression from section 5 with the spectrum factor already separated.
paragraph_plan: Separate the factor $e^{-j\omega\tau}$ from the remaining outer integrand.
Recognize the outer integral as $X(j\omega)$.
Combine the two named spectra to finish the proof idea.
Close by restating the theorem in the exact operational form needed for later lessons.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Recognize the separated factors in the transformed convolution expression and conclude that $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Finish the proof idea by naming the two individual spectra and combining them into the product form.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The final wrinkle is recognition rather than algebra: the student must match each factor to the corresponding Fourier transform.
solution_step_plan: Identify the outer integral as $X(j\omega)$.
Identify the inner factor as $H(j\omega)$.
Write the final product and restate the theorem in words.
practice_variation_axes: Rename the signals while keeping the same factorization.
Ask for the final theorem statement from a slightly different intermediate expression.
Vary whether the outer factor or inner factor is shown first in the expression.

sections.handoff_notes: End by making the recognition explicit and verbal: the student should say why the two named spectra multiply.

entries.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a continuous-time LTI convolution problem into Fourier-domain multiplication by finding X(j\omega) and H(j\omega), simplifying Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega), and inverse-transforming to recover y(t).

sections.section_title: Introduction to Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.learning_goal: Teach the shortcut: transform $x(t)$ and $h(t)$, multiply to get $Y(j\omega)$, then inverse-transform to recover $y(t)$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Establish that the convolution theorem replaces the direct integral $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ with the workflow $X(j\omega)$, $H(j\omega)$, $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, then inverse transform.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a simple LTI output where both $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ have standard transform pairs so the only new move is the theorem-driven shortcut.
paragraph_plan: State the direct-convolution problem and why it is expensive to compute by hand.
Name the convolution theorem and show the transform-domain correspondence between $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ and $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
Walk through the three-step workflow: transform the input and impulse response, multiply in frequency, then inverse-transform the product.
Close with the operational takeaway: use the theorem whenever convolution is the bottleneck and the transform pairs are available.

sections.handoff_notes: No practice in this section; the next step should immediately test recognition of the transform-domain relation.

sections.section_title: Translating a Convolution Output into Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)
sections.learning_goal: Given a time-domain convolution output, identify the exact frequency-domain equation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a time-domain statement that $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ for an LTI system, choose the correct frequency-domain relation for $Y(j\omega)$.
distractor_plan: Swap multiplication for addition in the frequency-domain relation.
Put the product on the wrong side of the equation or use the wrong output symbol.
Confuse the transform-domain relation with the inverse-transform step.
Drop one factor so the answer shows only $X(j\omega)$ or only $H(j\omega)$.
Write a time-domain convolution expression as if it still belonged in the frequency domain.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A system output is defined by $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$. Write the frequency-domain relation that lets you replace direct convolution with multiplication.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that transforming both signals turns convolution into the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete use of the theorem after the overview; no algebraic simplification yet, only the correct domain translation.
solution_step_plan: Identify the time-domain output as a convolution of the input and impulse response.
Apply the convolution theorem to transform the output into a product.
Label the transforms with the correct output symbol $Y(j\omega)$ and input factors $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$.
State the final frequency-domain relation cleanly without adding extra algebra.
practice_variation_axes: Change the notation for the input and impulse response while keeping the same convolution structure.
Hide the theorem inside a verbal description of an LTI output.
Ask for the transform-domain relation after a written convolution integral.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the question symbolic and notation-focused; no plots or transform tables are needed yet.

sections.section_title: Finding X(j\omega) and H(j\omega) from Transform Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Use known Fourier transform pairs to identify the transforms of $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ before forming $Y(j\omega)$.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given simple standard-pair signals $x(t)$ and $h(t)$, choose the correct $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ before forming $Y(j\omega)$.
distractor_plan: Use the transform pair for the wrong signal.
Omit a constant factor, amplitude scale, or time shift from one transform.
Confuse the input transform with the impulse-response transform.
Choose a pair that matches the general shape but not the exact parameter values.
Carry over a time-domain feature that should not appear in the frequency-domain pair.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given a simple input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$ with standard transform pairs, determine $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ and set up the product for $Y(j\omega)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to look up each transform pair correctly, including any constant factors or shifts, then write the product relation without skipping notation.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example only translated the theorem; this one adds transform-pair recognition for the two time-domain signals.
solution_step_plan: Identify each time-domain signal separately.
Match each signal to the correct Fourier transform pair.
Carry through any scaling, shifts, or sign conventions exactly.
Write $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, then form $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
practice_variation_axes: Use a shifted exponential or scaled pulse instead of the base signal.
Swap which signal is the input and which is the impulse response.
Include a factor that must be carried through the transform pair exactly.

sections.handoff_notes: The worked example should emphasize pair recognition over algebra; the next step is where simplification starts.

sections.section_title: Simplifying the Frequency-Domain Product Y(j\omega)
sections.learning_goal: Multiply $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ and simplify $Y(j\omega)$ into a form ready for inverse transformation.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given explicit expressions for $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, choose the simplified form of $Y(j\omega)$ that is ready for inverse transformation.
distractor_plan: Leave the product unsimplified so the correct pair is harder to see.
Drop a factor during cancellation or factoring.
Make a sign error in an exponent or denominator term.
Choose an expression that has the right ingredients but the wrong algebraic grouping.
Miss a constant that should be pulled outside the transform expression.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given explicit expressions for $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, multiply them and simplify the result to a form that can be inverse-transformed efficiently.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate clean algebraic simplification, including cancellation, factoring, and rewriting the result into a recognizable transform-pair shape.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The transforms are already known; the new work is algebraic cleanup of the product before inversion.
solution_step_plan: Multiply the transform expressions directly.
Simplify common factors, exponents, or denominators without changing the signal meaning.
Rewrite the product into a standard form that matches a known inverse-transform pair.
Check that the final expression is ready for the last time-domain step.
practice_variation_axes: Change the denominator structure so the simplification is not identical to the worked example.
Include a cancellation or repeated factor that must be handled cleanly.
Require factoring out a constant to expose a standard inverse-transform pair.

sections.handoff_notes: This step should read as algebraic cleanup after transform lookup, not as a new theorem.

sections.section_title: Inverse-Transforming Y(j\omega) to Recover y(t)
sections.learning_goal: Take a simplified $Y(j\omega)$ and recover $y(t)$ by matching inverse-transform pairs.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a simplified $Y(j\omega)$, choose the correct time-domain output $y(t)$ after inverse transformation.
distractor_plan: Use the wrong shift direction in the recovered time-domain signal.
Lose an amplitude factor during the inverse transform.
Confuse the inverse pair with the forward transform pair.
Pick an answer that matches the shape but not the exact parameter values.
Skip the rewrite needed to expose the standard inverse-transform pair.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given a simplified frequency-domain output $Y(j\omega)$, use inverse-transform pairs to recover the time-domain signal $y(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to match $Y(j\omega)$ to a known inverse pair and write the correct $y(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Now the product has been simplified; the remaining step is to identify the time-domain signal from the frequency-domain form.
solution_step_plan: Spot the standard inverse-transform pattern inside $Y(j\omega)$.
Handle any constants, shifts, or modulation factors correctly.
Apply the inverse transform to recover $y(t)$.
Verify that the result is written cleanly in the time domain.
practice_variation_axes: Use a different shift or modulation term.
Include a scale factor that must be pulled outside the transform.
Present a pair that must be recognized after a simple algebraic rewrite.

sections.handoff_notes: This step should focus on recognition of inverse-transform pairs and careful parameter handling.

sections.section_title: Applying the Full Shortcut to an LTI System Output
sections.learning_goal: Solve an entire LTI output problem by moving from $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ to $Y(j\omega)$ and back to $y(t)$ without direct convolution.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For a complete continuous-time LTI problem with given $x(t)$ and $h(t)$, choose the correct output $y(t)$ obtained by using the convolution theorem instead of evaluating the convolution integral.
distractor_plan: Combine mistakes from the earlier steps into plausible final outputs.
Use the wrong transform pair lookup for either $x(t)$ or $h(t)$.
Introduce an algebraic simplification error in $Y(j\omega)$.
Recover the wrong time-domain signal during the inverse transform.
Choose an output with the correct form but incorrect shift or scaling.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For a complete continuous-time LTI problem with given $x(t)$ and $h(t)$, find the output $y(t)$ using the convolution theorem instead of evaluating the convolution integral.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate the full workflow end to end: identify $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, multiply to get $Y(j\omega)$, simplify, and inverse-transform to recover $y(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This combines the earlier isolated moves into one complete problem with all steps chained together.
solution_step_plan: Translate both time-domain signals into their Fourier transforms.
Form the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
Simplify the product into a form that matches an inverse pair.
Inverse-transform the result and present the final time-domain output.
practice_variation_axes: Change one transform pair while keeping the workflow intact.
Alter the algebraic difficulty of $Y(j\omega)$.
Ask the student to decide when the shortcut is cleaner than direct convolution.

sections.handoff_notes: This final example should read like a complete worked shortcut, not a new theorem.
